Content:
A function [MATH: f: X \rightarrow Y] is said to be an into function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y] such that it has no preimage in [MATH: X.]

Content:
Symbolically, we can write:

Content:
> [MATH: f: X \to Y] is an into function if [MATH: \exists\, y \in Y] such that [MATH: \forall\, x \in X,] we have [MATH: f(x) \neq y.]

Content:
The following diagram shows an example of an into function.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/efb2be4674911446027a09ed031d4cc0]

Content:
According to the diagram, the element [MATH: 4 \in Y] has no preimage in [MATH: X] because we have no arrows from [MATH: X] to [MATH: 4.]So, we conclude that there exists some [MATH: y] (i.e., [MATH: y=4]) contained within [MATH: Y] such that [MATH: f(x) \neq y] for any [MATH: x] in [MATH: X.]

Content:
On the other hand, the following is not an into function because every element in [MATH: Y] has at least one element of [MATH: X] that maps to it.

2. [MATH: \exists\, y \in Y] such that [MATH: \forall\, x \in X,] we have [MATH: f(x) \neq y]
3. The function [MATH: f:X \to Y] is into

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that [MATH: f: X \rightarrow Y] is an into function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y] such that it has no preimage in [MATH: X\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: f: X \to Y] is an into function if [MATH: \exists\, y \in Y] such that [MATH: \forall\, x \in X,] we have [MATH: f(x) \neq y.]

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, there is an arrow from [MATH: 2 \in X] to [MATH: 4\in Y.] So, [MATH: f(2)=4.]

  • Statement II is true. According to the diagram, [MATH: 1 \in Y] has no preimage in [MATH: X] because we have no arrows from [MATH: X] to [MATH: 1 \in Y.] As a result, there exists some [MATH: y] (i.e., [MATH: y=1]) contained within [MATH: Y] such that [MATH: f(x) \neq y] for any [MATH: x] in [MATH: X.]

  • Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, [MATH: f] is an into function.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

Recall that [MATH: f: X \rightarrow Y] is an into function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y] such that it has no preimage in [MATH: X\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: f: X \to Y] is an into function if [MATH: \exists\, y \in Y] such that [MATH: \forall\, x \in X,] we have [MATH: f(x) \neq y.]

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is true. From the graph, the lowest [MATH: y]-value is [MATH: -2,] and it occurs at the point [MATH: (1,-2).] The graph will cover all [MATH: y]-values higher than [MATH: y=-2], including [MATH: y=-2] itself. So the range of the function is indeed [MATH: [-2, \infty).]

  • Statement II is true. Since the range of the function is [MATH: [-2, \infty)], then for all [MATH: y] contained within [MATH: [-2, \infty),] there exists some [MATH: x] contained within [MATH: \mathbb{R}] such that [MATH: f(x) = y.]

  • Statement III is true. As we can see from the range, there is no real number [MATH: x] such that [MATH: f(x)=-3 \in \mathbb{R}.] So, [MATH: f] maps [MATH: \mathbb{R}] into [MATH: \mathbb{R}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."

1. [MATH: f: [-2, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}] defined by [MATH: f(x) =\sqrt{ x+2}]
2. [MATH: g: \mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty)] defined by [MATH: g(x) = |x-2|+3]
3. [MATH: h:(0,\infty) \to\Bbb R] defined by [MATH: h(x) = \ln(x)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that [MATH: f: X \rightarrow Y] is an into function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y] such that it has no preimage in [MATH: X\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: f: X \to Y] is an into function if [MATH: \exists\, y \in Y] such that [MATH: \forall\, x \in X,] we have [MATH: f(x) \neq y.]

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

  • I is an into function. Let's take [MATH: -1 \in\Bbb R.] There is no number [MATH: x \in[-2, \infty)] such that [MATH: f(x) =\sqrt{ x+2}=-1.] In fact, [MATH: f(x) =\sqrt{ x+2} \geq 0] for all [MATH: x \in[-2, \infty) .]

  • II is an into function. Let's take [MATH: 1 \in [0, \infty).] There is no number [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] such that [MATH: g(x)=|x-2|+3=1.] In fact, [MATH: |x-2|+3 \geq 3] for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}.]

  • III is a not an into function. Given any [MATH: y \in \Bbb R,] we can choose [MATH: x =e^{y} \in \mathbb{R}.] Then [MATH: h(x) = h \left( e^{y}\right) =\ln(e^{y}) = y.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A function [MATH: f: X \rightarrow Y] is said to be an into function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y] such that it has no preimage in [MATH: X.]

Content:
Symbolically, we can write:

Content:
> [MATH: f: X \to Y] is an into function if [MATH: \exists\, y \in Y] such that [MATH: \forall\, x \in X,] we have [MATH: f(x) \neq y.]

Content:
The following diagram shows an example of an into function.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/efb2be4674911446027a09ed031d4cc0]

Content:
According to the diagram, the element [MATH: 4 \in Y] has no preimage in [MATH: X] because we have no arrows from [MATH: X] to [MATH: 4.]So, we conclude that there exists some [MATH: y] (i.e., [MATH: y=4]) contained within [MATH: Y] such that [MATH: f(x) \neq y] for any [MATH: x] in [MATH: X.]

Content:
On the other hand, the following is not an into function because every element in [MATH: Y] has at least one element of [MATH: X] that maps to it.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d2b47923e45556edac1418402f9d1f97]

---

Item 2 — Example: Functions Defined as Mapping Diagrams

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/43de28b75b644c83d8c2a11dc4dec6aa]

Which of the following statements are true regarding the function [MATH: f:X \to Y] represented by the mapping diagram above?

1. [MATH: f(2) = 4]
2. [MATH: \exists\, y \in Y] such that [MATH: \forall\, x \in X,] we have [MATH: f(x) \neq y]
3. The function [MATH: f:X \to Y] is into

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that [MATH: f: X \rightarrow Y] is an into function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y] such that it has no preimage in [MATH: X\mathbin{:}]

> [MATH: f: X \to Y] is an into function if [MATH: \exists\, y \in Y] such that [MATH: \forall\, x \in X,] we have [MATH: f(x) \neq y.]

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, there is an arrow from [MATH: 2 \in X] to [MATH: 4\in Y.] So, [MATH: f(2)=4.]
- Statement II is true. According to the diagram, [MATH: 1 \in Y] has no preimage in [MATH: X] because we have no arrows from [MATH: X] to [MATH: 1 \in Y.] As a result, there exists some [MATH: y] (i.e., [MATH: y=1]) contained within [MATH: Y] such that [MATH: f(x) \neq y] for any [MATH: x] in [MATH: X.]
- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, [MATH: f] is an into function.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

Item 5 — Example: Functions Whose Codomain Is the Set of Real Numbers

Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function [MATH: f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}] which is given by [MATH: f(x)=(x-1)^2-2?]

1. The range of [MATH: f] is [MATH: [-2, \infty)]
2. [MATH: \forall\, y \in [-2, \infty),] [MATH: \exists\, x \in \mathbb{R}] such that [MATH: f(x)=y]
3. [MATH: f] maps [MATH: \mathbb{R}] into [MATH: \mathbb{R}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we graph the function.

[IMG: /graphics/af001d95db33ac966a29b8f8e111cbc1]

Recall that [MATH: f: X \rightarrow Y] is an into function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y] such that it has no preimage in [MATH: X\mathbin{:}]

> [MATH: f: X \to Y] is an into function if [MATH: \exists\, y \in Y] such that [MATH: \forall\, x \in X,] we have [MATH: f(x) \neq y.]

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. From the graph, the lowest [MATH: y]-value is [MATH: -2,] and it occurs at the point [MATH: (1,-2).] The graph will cover all [MATH: y]-values higher than [MATH: y=-2], including [MATH: y=-2] itself. So the range of the function is indeed [MATH: [-2, \infty).]
- Statement II is true. Since the range of the function is [MATH: [-2, \infty)], then for all [MATH: y] contained within [MATH: [-2, \infty),] there exists some [MATH: x] contained within [MATH: \mathbb{R}] such that [MATH: f(x) = y.]
- Statement III is true. As we can see from the range, there is no real number [MATH: x] such that [MATH: f(x)=-3 \in \mathbb{R}.] So, [MATH: f] maps [MATH: \mathbb{R}] into [MATH: \mathbb{R}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."
